name: Bruck syndrome
aliases: osteogenesis imperfecta with congenital joint contractures

reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Tachdjian's Paediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder combining the bone fragility of osteogenesis imperfecta with congenital joint contractures
Presents with recurrent fractures, bone deformity, contractures (often of the elbows, knees and feet) and pterygia, with progressive scoliosis and short stature
Sclerae are usually normal or only mildly blue, helping distinguish it from classic osteogenesis imperfecta
Bruck syndrome type 1 is caused by FKBP10 variants and type 2 by PLOD2 variants, both affecting bone collagen cross-linking
Wormian bones and osteopenia are seen on radiographs alongside contractures
It should be considered in any child with both fragile bones and congenital contractures
Management combines fracture and bone-health care with physiotherapy, splinting and orthopaedic surgery for contractures and deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Bruck syndrome results from autosomal recessive variants in FKBP10 or PLOD2, genes whose products are required for the correct hydroxylation and cross-linking of type I collagen telopeptides in bone. PLOD2 encodes lysyl hydroxylase 2 and FKBP10 encodes a chaperone that supports its activity; deficiency produces abnormally cross-linked, mechanically weak bone collagen, giving the fragility and fractures of osteogenesis imperfecta. The same collagen abnormality, together with reduced foetal movement, contributes to the congenital joint contractures and pterygia, so the condition blends a bone-fragility disorder with an arthrogryposis phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita from other causes
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with fractures and joint involvement
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey showing fractures, osteopenia, deformity and Wormian bones
Molecular genetic testing for FKBP10 and PLOD2 and an osteogenesis imperfecta panel
Bone densitometry to quantify low bone mass
Assessment and monitoring of scoliosis and stature
Collagen biochemistry where genetic testing is inconclusive
Baseline calcium, phosphate and bone turnover markers before bone-directed therapy
redFlags: Recurrent fractures with minimal trauma, including at birth
Rapidly progressive scoliosis threatening respiratory function
Fracture during manipulation of contracted or fragile limbs
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; recurrent fractures, progressive deformity, scoliosis and short stature cause significant disability, though bone-protective care, rehabilitation and orthopaedic surgery can improve function, and cognition and lifespan are usually preserved.
pitfalls: Diagnosing plain osteogenesis imperfecta and overlooking the associated congenital contractures
Assuming blue sclerae must be present, when they are often normal in Bruck syndrome
Aggressive limb manipulation causing fractures in fragile bone
Neglecting scoliosis surveillance and bone-health management
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
